summary: Describes the widely deployed solution to the GRE fragmentation problem. It documents what vendors already do by default in the Internet, and the solution is configurable.

plainLanguage.summary: Putting a package inside another can make it too big for the truck. This records the way most companies fix it.

questions: when should i fragment the gre payload vs delivery packet
subtitle: How vendors solve the problem when tunneled packets are too large

tldr.problem: GRE tunnels wrap packets inside another header, making them larger. If the resulting packet is too large for the network path, fragmentation must happen—but the original GRE spec did not specify how.
tldr.mechanism: Vendors implemented a widely deployed solution that fragments the original packet before wrapping it in GRE (for IPv4), or fragments the outer tunnel packet (for IPv6), depending on whether the original packet can be fragmented.
tldr.outcome: This describes what vendors actually do by default, making it a de facto standard, though the solution has limits for IPv6 tunnels carrying large packets.

today: RFC 7588 documents the solution that vendors deployed widely in their GRE implementations. It is the consensus IETF approach to GRE fragmentation and remains the standard practice. The default configuration works well for most deployments but requires careful planning when IPv6 tunnels might encounter path MTUs below 1280 bytes.

sections.title: The GRE Tunneling Problem
sections.content:
Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) is a widely used tunneling protocol that wraps network-layer packets (IPv4, IPv6, or MPLS) inside another IP header for transport across the network. The problem is that this wrapping adds 4 to 24 bytes of header, making the resulting packet larger. If the wrapped packet exceeds the maximum size that the network path can carry (the Path MTU), the tunnel's ingress router must either discard it, fragment it, or fragment the outer packet.

The original GRE specification (RFC 2784 and RFC 2890) did not describe fragmentation procedures. Without guidance, different vendors implemented different solutions, causing interoperability problems. RFC 4459 identified several possible approaches. This RFC documents the solution that vendors actually deploy by default.
sections.plainLanguage: GRE wraps a packet like putting a box inside another box. If the outer box is too big for the truck, you have to break something up. Different companies were doing it differently, so this RFC records what most do.

sections.title: The Widely Deployed Solution
sections.content:
By default, most GRE implementations follow this logic: When an IPv4 packet that can be fragmented (the "Don't Fragment" bit is not set) arrives at the tunnel ingress and is larger than the tunnel's maximum transmission unit (GMTU), the ingress router fragments the original IPv4 packet first, then wraps each fragment in its own GRE header. The egress router receives complete, non-fragmented GRE packets, each containing a fragment, and forwards them to their final destination for reassembly.

When an IPv4 packet that cannot be fragmented arrives (the "Don't Fragment" bit is set), the ingress router discards it and sends back an ICMP "Fragmentation Needed" message, telling the sender to use a smaller packet size. For IPv6 packets (which cannot be fragmented by routers), the ingress router similarly discards oversized packets and sends back an ICMPv6 "Packet Too Big" message.

In non-default configurations, vendors also support fragmenting the outer GRE delivery packet instead, allowing it to be reassembled at the GRE egress node. This option is necessary for IPv6 tunnels when the GMTU cannot be guaranteed to be at least 1280 bytes, since IPv6 requires every link to support at least that size.
sections.plainLanguage: The normal approach: if the inner package is break-able, break it up before wrapping it. If it is not break-able or is IPv6, send back a message saying "make your packet smaller." Some setups allow breaking the outer wrapper instead.

sections.title: Practical Implementation Details
sections.content:
GRE ingress routers estimate the maximum size a packet can be to cross the tunnel (GMTU) by starting with the interface MTU toward the egress router and subtracting the GRE overhead (typically 4 to 24 bytes depending on GRE options and the IP version of the delivery header). Many routers refine this estimate using Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) to learn the actual maximum size that intermediate routers allow. However, PMTUD can be disabled for security reasons, since attackers can send forged ICMP messages claiming a smaller MTU.

When the GMTU changes due to network conditions or topology changes, the ingress router will not discover that immediately. This means the GMTU estimate may become inaccurate over time. The RFC emphasizes that operators should decide whether to fragment the GRE payload (so reassembly happens at the ultimate destination) or the GRE delivery packet (so reassembly happens at the egress router), based on where they prefer to place the computational burden of reassembly.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers guess how big a packet can be based on the network path. They can test it using a special technique called Path MTU Discovery. If they guess wrong sometimes, that is okay; the TCP protocol will adjust. But breaking things apart uses CPU, so you choose where to do it.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
Reassembling fragmented packets consumes router CPU and memory, and attackers can exploit this by sending fragmented packets faster than a router can reassemble them, or by sending overlapping fragments designed to confuse reassembly logic. Because of these risks, operators must decide whether to enable fragmentation at all, and if so, whether to reassemble at the egress router (where the tunnel ends) or at the ultimate destination.

Additionally, PMTUD is vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks: attackers can send forged ICMP messages telling routers that the path MTU is unusually small (causing excessive fragmentation) or unusually large (causing packets to be discarded). GRE implementations provide a configuration option to disable PMTUD and manually set the GMTU instead. The RFC references RFC 5722 for IPv6 and RFC 3128 for IPv4, which describe proper handling of overlapping fragments to mitigate some of these attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Breaking packets apart uses a lot of computer power and hackers can send fake packets designed to break routers. So you have to decide if the benefit of fragmentation is worth the risk, and have a way to turn it off if needed.

sections.title: Limitations and IPv6 Considerations
sections.content:
The default solution works well for IPv4 tunnels and is widely deployed. However, it has a limitation for IPv6: since IPv6 does not allow routers to fragment packets, and since RFC 2460 requires every IPv6 link to support at least 1280 bytes, the default solution is only appropriate for IPv6 tunnels if the network is engineered to guarantee a GMTU of at least 1280 bytes.

If the network cannot guarantee 1280 bytes—for example, in a tunnel over a network with unusual constraints—operators must switch to a non-default configuration that fragments the outer GRE delivery packet and reassembles it at the egress router. This configuration trades reassembly overhead for compatibility with IPv6's minimum MTU requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: For IPv6, this solution only works if every link in the tunnel can handle at least 1280 bytes. If not, you have to use a different approach that costs more CPU at the exit.
